Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX ) is reportedly planning to raise $40 billion in bank loans and investment-grade debt, led by Apollo Global Management (NYSE: APO ) , to buy Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ: NVDA ) chips.
The Elon Musk -led company is looking to raise about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt for the chip order, Reuters News reported, citing the Financial Times.

Apollo is expected to lead the deal and help place the debt with a broad range of investors, with Pimco among a small group of lenders in talks to provide financing, the newspaper reported citing people familiar with the matter.
The transaction is expected to close in 2027.
SpaceX, Apollo, and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Benzinga's request for comment, while Pimco declined to comment.

And if you spot something on sale, we have tips on how to actually save money during Prime Day . We’ve combed through hundreds of deals to find over 50 best audio deals. But if that’s too much, these are four deals I personally think are the best. We’ve spotted savings on earbuds, including the best discount we’ve seen on the AirPods Pro 2. Following the release of the latest Apple AirPods Pro 3 , the Pro 2 model is discounted. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 are among the best earbuds for Android users , even if you don’t have a Pixel phone. The Buds 3 have exceptional call and audio quality, and they play well within Samsung’s ecosystem. JBL’s affordable wireless earbuds lack noise canceling, but for less than $50, they’re a great value buy from a trusted audio brand. One of our favorite earbuds under $100 is even more affordable during Prime Day. The AeroClip earbuds are one of the best clip-on earbuds we’ve tested, combining comfort and sound quality. Shokz’s OpenDots One earbuds were among our favorite clip-on earbuds, thanks to their excellent sound and intuitive reversible fit. They’re $50 off right now. Nothing’s flagship Ear earbuds are on sale for just under $100, and they’re among the best-sounding earbuds , particularly for the price. Nothing’s affordable line of earbuds, CMF, just got more affordable. These feature a comfortable fit and surprisingly solid sound. Sony’s popular XM5 earbuds have excellent ANC and sound quality. Bose’s QuietComfort earbuds feature great ANC and sound, in a more budget-friendly package compared to the brand’s flagship earbuds. Beats’ Solo buds are pretty bare bones — there’s no ANC, and the case doesn’t have a battery — but they’re comfortable, lightweight, and have dependable physical controls. Headphones from Bose, Beats, Sonos, and more are all deeply discounted right now. Sony’s WH-1000XM4 are a couple of generations old now, but they’re still a great option. Bowers & Wilkins’ latest Px8 S2 headphones are a worthwhile upgrade, but an expensive one, according to our review. The last generation, which has the same excellent sound and design, is currently on sale. Beats’ affordable Solo 4 headphones are discounted to under $100 right now in multiple colors. From smart speakers to soundbars, these audio products will enhance your living space. Looking to take your home audio to the next level? Sony’s STRDH-190 stereo is ideal for turntables, TVs, and more. We want to hear it. Send us a tip using our anonymous form. Continue » The Roundhill Generative AI and Technology ETF (NYSEMKT: CHAT) exclusively invests in companies that are developing the hardware, software, and platforms powering the AI revolution. Investors can buy a single share in the ETF for under $100, and here's why it might be a good idea for the long term. Some ETFs hold hundreds or even thousands of individual stocks, but the Roundhill Generative AI and Technology ETF holds just 44. It has a highly concentrated portfolio because it invests solely in the AI industry, so investors shouldn't put all of their eggs in this basket alone. Instead, this fund would be a great addition to a diversified portfolio of other ETFs and individual stocks, particularly one that doesn't already have much exposure to the AI boom. The Roundhill ETF is quite top-heavy, with its 10 largest positions alone representing 39.4% of the value of its entire portfolio. However, they are some of the world's highest-quality AI companies. Alphabet, Microsoft, and Amazon are three of the biggest buyers of data center chips and components. They build AI infrastructure to develop their own models and software, but they also rent computing capacity via their respective cloud platforms to other businesses for a fee, which has become a very lucrative practice. The Roundhill Generative AI and Technology ETF launched in May 2023, so it doesn't have a very long track record for investors to analyze. However, it has soared by 267% since then, crushing the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 indexes which have returned 83% and 122%, respectively, over the same period. However, the AI industry is yet to hit a serious speed bump, so the Roundhill ETF hasn't been battle tested by a sustained downturn. Therefore, its past performance isn't necessarily a reliable indicator of its future results, which is all the more reason for investors to own it as part of a diversified portfolio. This strategy can still lead to strong returns, while keeping the potential risks in check. Cost is another consideration. The Roundhill ETF has an expense ratio of 0.75%, meaning investors will pay an annual fee of $75 for every $10,000 they park in the fund. That doesn't sound like much, but it's 25-times higher than what investors will pay in a typical Vanguard index fund , which is just 0.03%. High fees can chip away at investors' returns over the long term, which is a good argument for using a small position size. With all of that said, the Roundhill ETF can certainly be a great alternative to picking individual AI stocks. passages: Oct 6 (Reuters) - SpaceX plans to raise $40 billion, led by asset manager Apollo Global Management, for purchasing Nvidia AI chips, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Musk, who took SpaceX public in June in a record $86 billion IPO, had said last month that xAI's Colossus 2 data center could more than double the number of Nvidia chips it uses by December.

Nvidia, the dominant supplier of AI processors, in August partnered with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR on financing platforms intended to mobilize more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure projects.

Apollo is expected to lead the SpaceX deal and help place the debt with a broad range of investors, with bond fund Pimco among a small group of lenders in talks to provide financing, the newspaper reported, adding that the transaction is expected to close in 2027.
While SpaceX, Apollo and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment, Pimco declined to comment.
Shares of the rocket and spacecraft manufacturer fell 1% in extended trading after the report, while Nvidia's stock rose 0.5%.
The company plans to use Nvidia hardware exclusively to build its data centers, Musk said.

Nvidia, the dominant supplier of AI processors, in August partnered with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR on financing platforms intended to mobilize more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure projects. Apollo is expected to lead the SpaceX deal and help place the debt with a broad range of investors, with bond fund Pimco among a small group of lenders in talks to provide financing, the newspaper reported, adding that the transaction is expected to close in 2027. While SpaceX, Apollo and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment, Pimco declined to comment. Shares of the rocket and spacecraft manufacturer fell 1% in extended trading after the report, while Nvidia's stock rose 0.5%. The company plans to use Nvidia hardware exclusively to build its data centers, Musk said.

Oct 6 (Reuters) - SpaceX plans to raise $40 billion, led by asset manager Apollo Global Management, for purchasing Nvidia AI chips, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Musk, who took SpaceX public in June in a record $86 billion IPO, had said last month that xAI's Colossus 2 data center could more than double the number of Nvidia chips it uses by December.

Nvidia, the dominant supplier of AI processors, in August partnered with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR on financing platforms intended to mobilize more than $500 billion for AI infrastructure projects.

Apollo is expected to lead the SpaceX deal and help place the debt with a broad range of investors, with bond fund Pimco among a small group of lenders in talks to provide financing, the newspaper reported, adding that the transaction is expected to close in 2027.
While SpaceX, Apollo and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment, Pimco declined to comment.
Shares of the rocket and spacecraft manufacturer fell 1% in extended trading after the report, while Nvidia's stock rose 0.5%.
The company plans to use Nvidia hardware exclusively to build its data centers, Musk said.

Musk’s AI, satellite and rocket conglomerate is seeking to raise about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt to pay for the chips, the Financial Times reported earlier, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. Apollo Global Management Inc. is leading the financing, in a deal that is expected to close in 2027, the newspaper said. Tech companies and AI model developers are investing and borrowing hundreds of billions of dollars to build and lease giant data centers full of chips to power AI systems. Broadcom Inc.’s Wall Street syndicate is starting to gather $60 billion of fresh AI chip financing to benefit Anthropic PBC and other companies, people familiar with the matter said just days ago. Just last month, Musk said Colossus 2, an AI computing cluster built by his xAI business, may more than double its current Nvidia chip count by the end of the year. Colossus 2 now has 110,000 Nvidia GB200 chips and 440,000 GB300s, Musk said in a post on X. A further 220,000 GB300s are due to be operational next week, with another 220,000 expected in November, he said. An additional 220,000 may come online late December “if we get lucky,” he said. Apollo was among the US investment giants that Nvidia tapped for a high-profile partnership in August to source $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure. The coalition — which also includes Blackstone Inc., BlackRock Inc., Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and KKR & Co. — said at the time that they’d “create dedicated pools of capital at significant scale at attractive rates for Nvidia customers.” Executives indicated that it will focus on debt financing to provide access to compute for Nvidia’s largest customers and signaled that there were already many deals in the works that would qualify toward this commitment. Apollo has struck other deals with Elon Musk’s companies, including a $7 billion financing for xAI for access to Nvidia. The debt was earmarked for a special purpose vehicle to help Musk’s startup rent chips for its Colossus 2 data-center site in Memphis.

extraction.body: Advanced Navigation America, the US arm of global robotics company Advanced Navigation, is expanding manufacturing in Huntsville, Alabama, to scale high-precision navigation technology designed to keep mining equipment positioned and operating when GPS cannot be relied on. In mining, every decision impacts safety, efficiency, and continuous production. Yet across the industry, underground and surface operations remain tethered to vulnerable, legacy navigation infrastructure – relying on easily disrupted GPS signals that compromise accuracy and increase downtime. To close this technological gap, Advanced Navigation America, the US arm of global robotics company Advanced Navigation, is expanding manufacturing in Huntsville, Alabama, to build and deliver complex, high-precision mining navigation technology. Backed by US$110 million Series C round, this new Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) Centre of Excellence will research, develop, and manufacture deep technologies across fiber optics, MEMS, laser sensing, photonics, vision-based systems, AI, and quantum sensing. These technologies will help autonomous systems in mining and heavy industries maintain precise vehicle positioning in deep, dark, and unmapped environments where GPS cannot reach. It will also accelerate US mergers and acquisitions, bringing complementary technologies and expertise into the company’s portfolio. Together, these investments will expand the technologies available to mining operators, helping equipment navigate more precisely, operate in GPS-denied environments, and reduce reliance on human intervention in hazardous areas. “Resilient navigation and positioning is becoming the backbone of the autonomy shaping the future of mining and other heavy industries,” said Mike Cohen, President of Advanced Navigation America. “The challenge for America is making sure the industrial base can produce these vital technologies as quickly and reliably as demand is growing. That is the gap we are addressing in Huntsville: bringing high-performance manufacturing and faster delivery closer to the customers and industries that depend on it.” Technology that is extraordinarily difficult to make The hardest technology is often the most important technology to own. That makes the manufacturing technique itself part of the underlying intellectual property. With this extreme precision, FOG sensors excel in underground environments where GPS signals cannot reach. They are ideal for navigating haulage trucks, loaders, and Load-Haul-Dump (LHD) vehicles, as well as guiding high-accuracy production drill rigs. By delivering reliable, high-precision positioning underground, FOG technology enables robust fleet management, ensures strict chain-of-custody tracking, and verifies that ore is dumped in the correct locations. Advanced Navigation is one of a few companies globally with the capability to produce strategic-grade FOGs and laser velocity sensors at scale. These technologies provide the precision required for heavy industrial systems to understand where they are and how they are moving when GPS is degraded or unavailable across harsh environments. “With technology this precise, you can’t separate engineering from manufacturing,” said Chuck Matheny, Vice President of US Operations at Advanced Navigation America.“Production, calibration, and validation all have to work together. This means we can move beyond the limitations of legacy navigation tech and build for the applications driving industry today, and those still taking shape.”Huntsville: Turning hard science into American capabilityHuntsville was built around hard technology. Surrounded by Redstone Arsenal, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Centre and the country’s second-largest research park – the city is home to one of the highest concentrations of engineers and STEM workers per capita in the US. It has the specialist workforce and industrial base required to manufacture complex mining technologies.“Huntsville has spent generations turning hard science into American capability,” Cohen continued. “We’re putting the people who build and deploy this technology within minutes of our customers, changing how quickly we solve challenges, such as reducing operational downtime, and deploying safer, more efficient mining vehicles.” Built in America for miners Advanced Navigation was founded to solve one of autonomy’s hardest problems: how machines can navigate accurately when GPS cannot be relied upon. Today, its technology is deployed across land, air, sea, and space, ranging from deep underground mining and maritime operations to defense systems and lunar exploration. The company has more than 100 000 systems deployed globally, with customers spanning some of the world’s largest aerospace, defence, resources, and technology organisations including BHP, Fortescue, Leonardo, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and Intuitive Machines. The Huntsville facility establishes a major US manufacturing node alongside Advanced Navigation’s Australian and United Kingdom operational arms, enabling a trilateral production footprint across all three nations. This strengthens supply chain redundancy, increases global production capacity and allows Advanced Navigation America to respond faster to local US mining requirements. "The challenge isn't simply inventing better technology," said Cohen. "It's being able to manufacture it reliably, at scale, and get it into the hands of our customers to keep operations running. That is what we're building in Huntsville."“Our investment in our PNT Centre of Excellence gives our US customers direct access to the technology, engineering expertise and support they need for their most critical mining projects, backed by additional capability across Australia and the United Kingdom.” By turning deep technological breakthroughs into mass-producible, field-ready systems, Advanced Navigation America is equipping customers to operate with total confidence in the world’s most extreme environments.

extraction.body: Australian company Advanced Navigation has announced an expansion of its manufacturing capability into the USA, via the establishment of a positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) Centre of Excellence in Huntsville, Alabama. The expansion adds to the company’s existing manufacturing and R&D capabilities across NSW, WA and the ACT, which will remain the company’s core technology and manufacturing hubs. The new PNT Centre of Excellence will allow specific components, systems and builds to be produced on U.S. soil where required for security, classified programs or customer requirements. “Advanced Navigation was built in Australia, and [it] remains at the heart of our technology, engineering and manufacturing capability,” said Chris Shaw, CEO and co-founder of Advanced Navigation. “Expanding into the United States allows us to take that capability directly into one of the world’s largest defence and heavy industry markets. “It gives us additional capacity to support US programs while continuing to invest in the advanced manufacturing and R&D capability we have built here in Australia.” The company has made a name for itself through its fibre-optic gyroscope (FOG) inertial navigation systems (INS), which already have been or are being deployed in the defence, mining, aerospace, marine and autonomous systems sectors. The manufacture of FOG sensors precise enough to detect the Earth’s rotation requires engineering at a level similar to semiconductor fabrication, where even microscopic variations can affect performance. Advanced Navigation is one of a few companies globally with the capability to produce strategic-grade FOGs and laser velocity sensors at scale. “With technology this precise, you can’t separate engineering from manufacturing,” said Chuck Matheny, Vice President of U.S. Operations at Advanced Navigation America. “Production, calibration and validation all have to work together. The capability developed in Australia gives us a strong foundation to build from as we establish dedicated manufacturing in Huntsville and respond to the specific requirements of US defence programs.” The new Huntsville PNT Centre of Excellence will focus on advanced manufacturing, adding dedicated US production capacity alongside the company’s Australian operations. The facility will support the production of technologies spanning fibre optics, MEMS and photonics, while enabling Advanced Navigation to undertake US-based production where required for sensitive and classified defence programs or customer requirements. “Our investment in Huntsville is an extension of what we have built in Australia, not a replacement for it,” said Shaw. “This is about an Aussie deep-tech company taking its technology and manufacturing capability into one of the world’s largest defence and heavy industry markets, while continuing to invest, innovate and manufacture here at home.” fibre-optic gyroscope , hero , navigation , PNT , positioning , timing © 2026 Spatial Source. Backed by US$110 million Series C round, this new Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) Centre of Excellence will research, develop, and manufacture deep technologies across fiber optics, MEMS, laser sensing, photonics, vision-based systems, AI, and quantum sensing. These technologies will help autonomous systems in mining and heavy industries maintain precise vehicle positioning in deep, dark, and unmapped environments where GPS cannot reach. It will also accelerate US mergers and acquisitions, bringing complementary technologies and expertise into the company’s portfolio. Together, these investments will expand the technologies available to mining operators, helping equipment navigate more precisely, operate in GPS-denied environments, and reduce reliance on human intervention in hazardous areas. “Resilient navigation and positioning is becoming the backbone of the autonomy shaping the future of mining and other heavy industries,” said Mike Cohen, President of Advanced Navigation America. “The challenge for America is making sure the industrial base can produce these vital technologies as quickly and reliably as demand is growing. That is the gap we are addressing in Huntsville: bringing high-performance manufacturing and faster delivery closer to the customers and industries that depend on it.” Technology that is extraordinarily difficult to make The hardest technology is often the most important technology to own. That makes the manufacturing technique itself part of the underlying intellectual property. With this extreme precision, FOG sensors excel in underground environments where GPS signals cannot reach. They are ideal for navigating haulage trucks, loaders, and Load-Haul-Dump (LHD) vehicles, as well as guiding high-accuracy production drill rigs. By delivering reliable, high-precision positioning underground, FOG technology enables robust fleet management, ensures strict chain-of-custody tracking, and verifies that ore is dumped in the correct locations. Advanced Navigation is one of a few companies globally with the capability to produce strategic-grade FOGs and laser velocity sensors at scale. This strengthens supply chain redundancy, increases global production capacity and allows Advanced Navigation America to respond faster to local US mining requirements. Advanced Navigation has already begun hiring to fill some 75 to 100 positions across engineering, manufacturing and operations as it builds out the facility. The technology will help autonomous systems navigate the world’s harshest environments when GPS cannot be relied on. Building fiber optic gyroscope sensors precise enough to detect the Earth’s rotation requires engineering at a level similar to semiconductor fabrication, where even microscopic variations can affect performance. extraction.body: (Oct 7): Cryptocurrencies fell on Wednesday as a wave of forced selling swept across digital-asset venues, with broader market jitters further weighing on risk appetite. Bitcoin, the largest token, fell as much as 2.5% to US$83,470 while ether slumped 4.9% to US$2,567. Other smaller digital assets also fell, with XRP and Solana down 4.2% and 3.4% respectively. The retreat accelerated as leveraged bets were unwound, with around US$609 million in crypto positions liquidated over the last 24 hours, according to Coinglass data. “The dip in crypto prices serves as a leverage flush instead of a downward trend, stemming from crowded bets on higher prices being forced out, with most of the liquidations coming from long positions,” said Dan Khus, chief analyst at LVRG Research. The crypto losses reflected a broader cooling in appetite for risk as renewed Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz tempered hopes that shipping through the key waterway may return to pre-war levels, pushing Brent crude above US$101 a barrel. US stocks' futures edged lower after the S&P 500 closed at an all-time high in the prior session. Europe’s Stoxx 600 snapped three straight days of gains while a recovery in bonds also lost steam, with the 10-year Treasury yield climbing above 5.3%. Traders are watching the release of Federal Reserve meeting minutes later on Wednesday for clues to the outlook for interest rates, said Rachael Lucas, an analyst at BTC Markets. “A hawkish read could lift yields and the US dollar, keeping pressure on risk assets,” Lucas said. The slump in crypto prices comes after a recovery from bitcoin’s summer lows, although it remains well off its peak of US$126,000 a year ago. Trading may remain choppy for the rest of the week in the absence of a fresh catalyst, according to Pratik Kala, a portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto. “If we lose US$83,000, it is possible we revisit the US$78,000 region for bitcoin, which should provide some support,” he said. Other smaller digital assets also fell, with XRP and Solana down 4.2% and 3.4% respectively.
The retreat accelerated as leveraged bets were unwound, with around US$609 million in crypto positions liquidated over the last 24 hours, according to Coinglass data.

“The dip in crypto prices serves as a leverage flush instead of a downward trend, stemming from crowded bets on higher prices being forced out, with most of the liquidations coming from long positions,” said Dan Khus, chief analyst at LVRG Research.

Bitcoin, the largest token, fell as much as 2.5% to US$83,470 while ether slumped 4.9% to US$2,567. Other smaller digital assets also fell, with XRP and Solana down 4.2% and 3.4% respectively. The retreat accelerated as leveraged bets were unwound, with around US$609 million in crypto positions liquidated over the last 24 hours, according to Coinglass data. “The dip in crypto prices serves as a leverage flush instead of a downward trend, stemming from crowded bets on higher prices being forced out, with most of the liquidations coming from long positions,” said Dan Khus, chief analyst at LVRG Research. The crypto losses reflected a broader cooling in appetite for risk as renewed Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz tempered hopes that shipping through the key waterway may return to pre-war levels, pushing Brent crude above US$101 a barrel. US stocks' futures edged lower after the S&P 500 closed at an all-time high in the prior session. Europe’s Stoxx 600 snapped three straight days of gains while a recovery in bonds also lost steam, with the 10-year Treasury yield climbing above 5.3%. Traders are watching the release of Federal Reserve meeting minutes later on Wednesday for clues to the outlook for interest rates, said Rachael Lucas, an analyst at BTC Markets. “A hawkish read could lift yields and the US dollar, keeping pressure on risk assets,” Lucas said. The slump in crypto prices comes after a recovery from bitcoin’s summer lows, although it remains well off its peak of US$126,000 a year ago. Trading may remain choppy for the rest of the week in the absence of a fresh catalyst, according to Pratik Kala, a portfolio manager at Apollo Crypto. “If we lose US$83,000, it is possible we revisit the US$78,000 region for bitcoin, which should provide some support,” he said. passages: If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads.

extraction.body: As decision models spread across the industry, a company called Musubi has a new idea for how to put them to work: moderating content. On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B , released with open weights. The idea is to take a content policy written in plain English and apply it to messages in under 50 milliseconds. Musubi’s model is designed to be similar in cost and speed to the AI classifier systems that power moderation on most social platforms — but because it has the flexibility of a modern LLM, it can apply complex policies without special training. Even more important, the model won’t need new training when the policy changes, allowing for human policy-setters to iterate as much as they need. As Musubi co-founder and chief AI officer Filip Jankovic sees it, it gives platform managers a way to label content proactively. “Product teams just want a better understanding of what’s happening on their platform, especially as the amount of content is exponentially increasing,” Jankovic says. “Being able to label all of that in a very scalable, customizable way is extremely useful.” Decision models have become a hot topic in the AI world since the release of TypeSafe AI’s Jev in September , which was shortly followed by competing decision models from OpenAI and Amazon . Instead of outputting text, a decision model outputs outcome probabilities, though in this case the model outputs a binary judgement: Either the content is in the category or it isn’t. By limiting the model’s output to a set of predetermined choices, decision models are able to run faster and cheaper than large language models, while still maintaining the flexibility of the transformer architecture. One early use case is reining in misbehavior by AI agents — so it’s only natural to apply the same technology to human misbehavior. Notably, Jankovic says his interest in decision models predates Jev, tracing it back to a 2024 project called GLiNER (Generalist Model for Named Entity Recognition) that deployed many of the same techniques. Still, Musubi isn’t wary of the comparison. If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads. sources.title: Acurast brings real time AI decision model Laya to smartphone network
passages: Acurast has deployed open source AI decision model Laya across its decentralized smartphone compute network, allowing the model to process real time decisions on Android devices instead of centralized data centers.

According to Acurast the deployment runs Laya entirely on mobile edge nodes and uses the network’s distributed smartphones to handle workloads including classification, gaming, navigation, security and content moderation.

Smartphones handle the AI workloads without GPUs Acurast said decisions in its Laya deployment typically take roughly 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs rather than dedicated GPUs.
More than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the Acurast network, according to the company.
“By running Laya on Acurast, we’ve changed that,” Acurast founder Alessandro De Carli said.
Crypto.news previously reported that Acurast raised $5.4 million in May 2025 to develop its smartphone powered decentralized cloud network.
Convai Innovations describes Laya as a “System 1” decision model built for tasks where an application needs a quick structured response.
Acurast said it has tested Laya for detecting prompt injection attempts against AI assistants and identifying toxic messages in live chats.

“We are proving that System 1 AI can run securely and at scale on hardware everyone already owns, providing a truly open, decentralized alternative to centralized cloud lock-in.” Laya’s public code and model weights are available under the Apache 2.0 license.
Laya processes structured decisions for gaming, classification, moderation and security tasks instead of generating conversational text.
Results come with cryptographic proof, while smartphone operators receive ACU, Acurast’s native token, for providing processing capacity.
Gaia introduced an AI smartphone in September 2025 that was designed to run AI locally on the device while letting users contribute compute to its decentralized network.
For gaming, Laya has been used to play Snake and Tetris by choosing movements and determining where falling pieces should be placed.
Laya’s developers have documented limitations as well.
Acurast’s approach relies on existing consumer hardware instead of requiring operators to purchase dedicated servers or GPUs.

extraction.body: Acurast has deployed open source AI decision model Laya across its decentralized smartphone compute network, allowing the model to process real time decisions on Android devices instead of centralized data centers. Acurast has deployed open source Laya AI across its decentralized smartphone compute network. Laya processes structured decisions for gaming, classification, moderation and security tasks instead of generating conversational text. Acurast said decisions typically take around 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs without dedicated GPUs. More than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the Acurast network, according to the company. According to Acurast the deployment runs Laya entirely on mobile edge nodes and uses the network’s distributed smartphones to handle workloads including classification, gaming, navigation, security and content moderation. Acurast brings Laya AI model to smartphone compute network Laya, developed by Convai Innovations under an Apache 2.0 license, is designed to make structured decisions instead of generating conversational responses. Given a defined state and a set of possible actions, the model evaluates the input and selects an option. Its open source repository describes three main decision formats covering choices between defined options, scoring against a set range and boolean decisions. The model uses a non autoregressive architecture, meaning it does not generate an answer token by token in the way large language models typically produce text. Convai Innovations describes Laya as a “System 1” decision model built for tasks where an application needs a quick structured response. Acurast is using the model to demonstrate how such workloads can operate across commodity mobile hardware. Each decision in its deployment is processed on an Android smartphone connected to the network, according to the company. “By running Laya on Acurast, we’ve changed that,” Acurast founder Alessandro De Carli said. “We are proving that System 1 AI can run securely and at scale on hardware everyone already owns, providing a truly open, decentralized alternative to centralized cloud lock-in.” Laya’s public code and model weights are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Its repository lists a 421 million parameter English checkpoint, alongside separate models for multilingual and typed decision workloads. Acurast has set up several live demonstrations to test the model across different types of decision based tasks. For gaming, Laya has been used to play Snake and Tetris by choosing movements and determining where falling pieces should be placed. A Doom demonstration requires the model to make decisions around movement, aiming, shooting, collecting items and exploring the game environment. The model can classify emails as inbox messages, spam or phishing attempts and sort headlines into categories including news, satire, clickbait and manipulation. Acurast said it has tested Laya for detecting prompt injection attempts against AI assistants and identifying toxic messages in live chats. Users can submit their own letters, headlines, prompts and other inputs to the demonstrations and observe the decisions made by the model. Laya’s developers have documented limitations as well. The project’s repository says its general model performs poorly on some zero shot typed decision tests and recommends specializing the model for specific tasks. It advises keeping choice questions below roughly 20 options and recalibrating probabilities using application specific data. Smartphones handle the AI workloads without GPUs Acurast said decisions in its Laya deployment typically take roughly 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs rather than dedicated GPUs. Work is distributed dynamically between devices participating in the network. Results come with cryptographic proof, while smartphone operators receive ACU, Acurast’s native token, for providing processing capacity. The network uses Trusted Execution Environments built into modern smartphones to isolate workloads and protect data while computation takes place, according to Acurast. Acurast’s approach relies on existing consumer hardware instead of requiring operators to purchase dedicated servers or GPUs. The company has previously applied the same model to blockchain infrastructure and other decentralized computing workloads. Crypto.news previously reported that Acurast raised $5.4 million in May 2025 to develop its smartphone powered decentralized cloud network. At the time, the network had more than 72,000 smartphones and had processed 256 million transactions. Acurast now says more than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the network, while the number of on chain transactions processed has passed 918 million. The model fits into a growing effort to use consumer devices for decentralized AI workloads. Gaia introduced an AI smartphone in September 2025 that was designed to run AI locally on the device while letting users contribute compute to its decentralized network.

extraction.body: As decision models spread across the industry, a company called Musubi has a new idea for how to put them to work: moderating content. On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B , released with open weights. The idea is to take a content policy written in plain English and apply it to messages in under 50 milliseconds. Musubi’s model is designed to be similar in cost and speed to the AI classifier systems that power moderation on most social platforms — but because it has the flexibility of a modern LLM, it can apply complex policies without special training. Even more important, the model won’t need new training when the policy changes, allowing for human policy-setters to iterate as much as they need. As Musubi co-founder and chief AI officer Filip Jankovic sees it, it gives platform managers a way to label content proactively. “Product teams just want a better understanding of what’s happening on their platform, especially as the amount of content is exponentially increasing,” Jankovic says. “Being able to label all of that in a very scalable, customizable way is extremely useful.” Decision models have become a hot topic in the AI world since the release of TypeSafe AI’s Jev in September , which was shortly followed by competing decision models from OpenAI and Amazon . Instead of outputting text, a decision model outputs outcome probabilities, though in this case the model outputs a binary judgement: Either the content is in the category or it isn’t. By limiting the model’s output to a set of predetermined choices, decision models are able to run faster and cheaper than large language models, while still maintaining the flexibility of the transformer architecture. One early use case is reining in misbehavior by AI agents — so it’s only natural to apply the same technology to human misbehavior. Notably, Jankovic says his interest in decision models predates Jev, tracing it back to a 2024 project called GLiNER (Generalist Model for Named Entity Recognition) that deployed many of the same techniques. Still, Musubi isn’t wary of the comparison. If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads. extraction.body: Acurast has deployed open source AI decision model Laya across its decentralized smartphone compute network, allowing the model to process real time decisions on Android devices instead of centralized data centers. Acurast has deployed open source Laya AI across its decentralized smartphone compute network. Laya processes structured decisions for gaming, classification, moderation and security tasks instead of generating conversational text. Acurast said decisions typically take around 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs without dedicated GPUs. More than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the Acurast network, according to the company. According to Acurast the deployment runs Laya entirely on mobile edge nodes and uses the network’s distributed smartphones to handle workloads including classification, gaming, navigation, security and content moderation. Acurast brings Laya AI model to smartphone compute network Laya, developed by Convai Innovations under an Apache 2.0 license, is designed to make structured decisions instead of generating conversational responses. Given a defined state and a set of possible actions, the model evaluates the input and selects an option. Its open source repository describes three main decision formats covering choices between defined options, scoring against a set range and boolean decisions. The model uses a non autoregressive architecture, meaning it does not generate an answer token by token in the way large language models typically produce text. Convai Innovations describes Laya as a “System 1” decision model built for tasks where an application needs a quick structured response. Acurast is using the model to demonstrate how such workloads can operate across commodity mobile hardware. Each decision in its deployment is processed on an Android smartphone connected to the network, according to the company. “By running Laya on Acurast, we’ve changed that,” Acurast founder Alessandro De Carli said. “We are proving that System 1 AI can run securely and at scale on hardware everyone already owns, providing a truly open, decentralized alternative to centralized cloud lock-in.” Laya’s public code and model weights are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Its repository lists a 421 million parameter English checkpoint, alongside separate models for multilingual and typed decision workloads. Acurast has set up several live demonstrations to test the model across different types of decision based tasks. For gaming, Laya has been used to play Snake and Tetris by choosing movements and determining where falling pieces should be placed. A Doom demonstration requires the model to make decisions around movement, aiming, shooting, collecting items and exploring the game environment. The model can classify emails as inbox messages, spam or phishing attempts and sort headlines into categories including news, satire, clickbait and manipulation. Acurast said it has tested Laya for detecting prompt injection attempts against AI assistants and identifying toxic messages in live chats. Users can submit their own letters, headlines, prompts and other inputs to the demonstrations and observe the decisions made by the model. Laya’s developers have documented limitations as well. The project’s repository says its general model performs poorly on some zero shot typed decision tests and recommends specializing the model for specific tasks. It advises keeping choice questions below roughly 20 options and recalibrating probabilities using application specific data. Smartphones handle the AI workloads without GPUs Acurast said decisions in its Laya deployment typically take roughly 0.2 to 1 second and are processed using smartphone CPUs rather than dedicated GPUs. Work is distributed dynamically between devices participating in the network. Results come with cryptographic proof, while smartphone operators receive ACU, Acurast’s native token, for providing processing capacity. The network uses Trusted Execution Environments built into modern smartphones to isolate workloads and protect data while computation takes place, according to Acurast. Acurast’s approach relies on existing consumer hardware instead of requiring operators to purchase dedicated servers or GPUs. The company has previously applied the same model to blockchain infrastructure and other decentralized computing workloads. Crypto.news previously reported that Acurast raised $5.4 million in May 2025 to develop its smartphone powered decentralized cloud network. At the time, the network had more than 72,000 smartphones and had processed 256 million transactions. Acurast now says more than 280,000 smartphones across over 175 countries have joined the network, while the number of on chain transactions processed has passed 918 million. The model fits into a growing effort to use consumer devices for decentralized AI workloads. Gaia introduced an AI smartphone in September 2025 that was designed to run AI locally on the device while letting users contribute compute to its decentralized network.

extraction.body: Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer. But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job. Most recently, Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog. However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity. What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction. For instance, TechCrunch has seen a han d ful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. ( NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.) But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences. The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out. It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into. To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post. This is frustrating. @Walmart in their attempt to stop agent from making purchases has gone too far and is essentially blocking actual human from making purchase on their website. I tried to purchase something directly and I can't even sign in. pic.twitter.com/CRAgkrCCa0 Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology. For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests. Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.” “While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained. United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.) Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp , eBay , Zillow , Pizza Hut , Adidas , and various airlines . Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently increased . A couple of people even said eBay suspended their accounts because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that Google kicked out Instinct while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them. Looks like @adidas won't get my business tonight 😪 pic.twitter.com/DXcPYE5S6O Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its data licensing program . That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp. eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training. Adidas, Zillow, and Pizza Hut either didn’t respond or declined to provide a comment by the time of publication. One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads. However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar . The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones. Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it now runs a marketplace where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing a new web browser built specifically for AI agents. Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs. Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s newly announced partners haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid expansion , which now includes partnered tools for small businesses , a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”

extraction.body: Ninety-seven percent of top websites aren’t ready for AI agents, according to research from BrightEdge, an AI-powered organic search provider. But these agents are here, and they are banging on your website’s door. Is there a way to let them in without rebuilding your website to meet their needs? BrightEdge says yes, and it has it. BrightEdge says that for every 100 visits a site receives from human organic search, it receives, on average, 88 from AI agents, the bulk of which are from OpenAI. AI Agents have become digital assistants that help people get the information they need, including researching products, comparing options, and checking product availability. These agents don’t just hit your website once; instead, they often make multiple trips to your site to get everything they need for the end user. Says BrightEdge: For digital marketers, that number [95% of agent interactions come from OpenAI] has a practical implication that goes beyond strategy. If you haven't already had conversations with your IT, dev, or ops teams about AI agents, there's a good chance those agents are currently being treated the same as any other bot -- meaning they may be throttled, blocked, or otherwise restricted from reaching your content. The systems that control this sit outside of marketing's hands, and closing that gap sooner rather than later is no longer optional. Your website needs to support these agents. You can’t block them; they are your window to get found in AI search or to help a ChatGPT user (or other AI assistant) answer questions about your brand and products. But you also don’t necessarily want them to come to your website and take forever to find the information they need. Agents work best with simplicity. They like structure - like Markdown (a lightweight, structured text format that strips away much of the presentation and scripting of a normal web page). And your website is not written in Markdown. BrightEdge says that AI agents are creating a “second web.” The second web is a new layer of access that creates a second audience for your content. How well you create that second web (and how you do it) affects the quality of the interactions between agents and your content. From June 2025 to June 2026, BrightEdge analyzed ChatGPT recommendations across nine industries. It found that ChatGPT researched more but recommended brands less. As Jim Yu, CEO and co-founder of BrightEdge, notes: AI agents are getting dramatically better at doing the work people once had to do themselves.They are researching, comparing and taking action on our behalf, making the point of interaction between an agent and a brand increasingly critical. The companies that can understand and optimize those interactions will have a significant advantage as this second audience grows. While it is important to ensure agents can get the right information, it’s not necessarily critical that information is delivered in Markdown format. For agents that specifically request it, yes, it needs to be available, but most agents can read a traditional web page fine, as long as it’s structured properly. In fact, Profound did an experiment to see if serving Markdown to agents improved a brand’s visibility in AI search. It looked at 381 pages across six websites, with half the pages serving HTML and half serving Markdown to AI agents.Here’s what it found: At first glance, the Markdown group looks slightly ahead: one more median visit per page, about 16% higher on average. But here's the catch: the median page (your typical page) only got one extra visit. The 16% mean difference is driven almost entirely by high-traffic pages in the tail of the distribution, pages that were already getting lots of bot attention saw modest gains, while the median page saw almost nothing. [..] Put simply: we can't say with confidence that Markdown actually drove more traffic. There’s more to supporting AI agents than implementing a schema, but that’s what most brands are doing today, says BrightEdge. Very few are taking the next step of serving content specially designed to support agent queries. That being said, Search Engine Optimization (SEO) tool providers are giving brands the tools they need to support AI agents, including BrightEdge. Here are a couple of them. Agent Edge looks for agent requests at the Content Delivery Network (CDN) layer. When it gets an agent request, it serves content to the agent in Markdown, reducing the number of tokens an agent uses. The Markdown versions are copies of the HTML web pages with all the extra stuff taken out (like navigation, JavaScript, and so on). Marketers have a dashboard where they can select the web pages they want converted to Markdown, and Agent Edge will create the Markdown version (marketers can make edits as well). BrightEdge goes further, though, because Agent Edge can use BrightEdge Intelligence to anticipate follow-on questions the agent is likely to ask and build on the initial content with those answers. Enriching the response with additional important information means the agent doesn’t have to come back and request more information. What’s nice about BrightEdge is that you get SEO, AI search, and agent interactions in one platform, allowing you to see and optimize holistically across all three. seoClarity also tracks AI agents and delivers content optimized as Markdown. Like BrightEdge, it is implemented at the CDN layer, intercepting all requests and delivering Markdown if an agent requests it (it’s called HTTP Content Negotiation). Brands can select which web pages to convert to Markdown and approve the Markdown version. Both the HTML and Markdown versions of a web page share the same canonical URL, making it easy to track and analyze traffic, with full auditability and logging. Cloudflare isn’t an SEO provider; it is an internet infrastructure and security company. A CDN is one of the products it provides. It also uses HTTP Content Negotiation, so when an agent sends a request and asks for a Markdown response, Cloudflare converts the web page in real time at the source and delivers it to the agent. To help brands learn how much Markdown is being delivered, Cloudflare added a content type to its Radar product, allowing marketers to see AI bot and crawler traffic. The more tools we have that help brands understand how to get found in AI search, the better. But marketers need to be careful and ask lots of questions about how features work and what results they can expect. And tool providers need to prove why they work the way they do. BrightEdge can track how AI agents interact with brands, what those agents are trying to access, and how that behavior is changing. That means they can show a brand the before-and-after of implementing Agent Edge. This is the kind of information brands need from their tool providers to know their investment is warranted. diginomica and the diginomica logo are trademarks of diginomica Limited. © Diginomica Limited and its licensors 2013- 2026

Agents work best with simplicity. They like structure - like Markdown (a lightweight, structured text format that strips away much of the presentation and scripting of a normal web page). And your website is not written in Markdown. BrightEdge says that AI agents are creating a “second web.” The second web is a new layer of access that creates a second audience for your content.
How well you create that second web (and how you do it) affects the quality of the interactions between agents and your content.
From June 2025 to June 2026, BrightEdge analyzed ChatGPT recommendations across nine industries. It found that ChatGPT researched more but recommended brands less.
As Jim Yu, CEO and co-founder of BrightEdge, notes:

AI agents are getting dramatically better at doing the work people once had to do themselves.They are researching, comparing and taking action on our behalf, making the point of interaction between an agent and a brand increasingly critical. The companies that can understand and optimize those interactions will have a significant advantage as this second audience grows.

While it is important to ensure agents can get the right information, it’s not necessarily critical that information is delivered in Markdown format. For agents that specifically request it, yes, it needs to be available, but most agents can read a traditional web page fine, as long as it’s structured properly.

In fact, Profound did an experiment to see if serving Markdown to agents improved a brand’s visibility in AI search. It looked at 381 pages across six websites, with half the pages serving HTML and half serving Markdown to AI agents.Here’s what it found:

At first glance, the Markdown group looks slightly ahead: one more median visit per page, about 16% higher on average. But here's the catch: the median page (your typical page) only got one extra visit. The 16% mean difference is driven almost entirely by high-traffic pages in the tail of the distribution, pages that were already getting lots of bot attention saw modest gains, while the median page saw almost nothing. [..] Put simply: we can't say with confidence that Markdown actually drove more traffic.

There’s more to supporting AI agents than implementing a schema, but that’s what most brands are doing today, says BrightEdge. Very few are taking the next step of serving content specially designed to support agent queries. That being said, Search Engine Optimization (SEO) tool providers are giving brands the tools they need to support AI agents, including BrightEdge. Here are a couple of them.

Agent Edge looks for agent requests at the Content Delivery Network (CDN) layer. When it gets an agent request, it serves content to the agent in Markdown, reducing the number of tokens an agent uses. The Markdown versions are copies of the HTML web pages with all the extra stuff taken out (like navigation, JavaScript, and so on). Marketers have a dashboard where they can select the web pages they want converted to Markdown, and Agent Edge will create the Markdown version (marketers can make edits as well).

BrightEdge goes further, though, because Agent Edge can use BrightEdge Intelligence to anticipate follow-on questions the agent is likely to ask and build on the initial content with those answers. Enriching the response with additional important information means the agent doesn’t have to come back and request more information.
What’s nice about BrightEdge is that you get SEO, AI search, and agent interactions in one platform, allowing you to see and optimize holistically across all three.

seoClarity also tracks AI agents and delivers content optimized as Markdown. Like BrightEdge, it is implemented at the CDN layer, intercepting all requests and delivering Markdown if an agent requests it (it’s called HTTP Content Negotiation).

Brands can select which web pages to convert to Markdown and approve the Markdown version. Both the HTML and Markdown versions of a web page share the same canonical URL, making it easy to track and analyze traffic, with full auditability and logging.

Cloudflare isn’t an SEO provider; it is an internet infrastructure and security company. A CDN is one of the products it provides. It also uses HTTP Content Negotiation, so when an agent sends a request and asks for a Markdown response, Cloudflare converts the web page in real time at the source and delivers it to the agent.
To help brands learn how much Markdown is being delivered, Cloudflare added a content type to its Radar product, allowing marketers to see AI bot and crawler traffic.

The more tools we have that help brands understand how to get found in AI search, the better. But marketers need to be careful and ask lots of questions about how features work and what results they can expect. And tool providers need to prove why they work the way they do.

BrightEdge can track how AI agents interact with brands, what those agents are trying to access, and how that behavior is changing. That means they can show a brand the before-and-after of implementing Agent Edge. This is the kind of information brands need from their tool providers to know their investment is warranted.

extraction.body: Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer. But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job. Most recently, Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog. However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity. What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction. For instance, TechCrunch has seen a han d ful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. ( NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.) But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences. The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out. It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into. To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post. This is frustrating. @Walmart in their attempt to stop agent from making purchases has gone too far and is essentially blocking actual human from making purchase on their website. I tried to purchase something directly and I can't even sign in. pic.twitter.com/CRAgkrCCa0 Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology. For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests. Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.” “While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained. United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.) Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp , eBay , Zillow , Pizza Hut , Adidas , and various airlines . Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently increased . A couple of people even said eBay suspended their accounts because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that Google kicked out Instinct while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them. Looks like @adidas won't get my business tonight 😪 pic.twitter.com/DXcPYE5S6O Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its data licensing program . That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp. eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training. Adidas, Zillow, and Pizza Hut either didn’t respond or declined to provide a comment by the time of publication. One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads. However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar . The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones. Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it now runs a marketplace where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing a new web browser built specifically for AI agents. Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs. Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s newly announced partners haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid expansion , which now includes partnered tools for small businesses , a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway. “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”

One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads.

However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar . The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones.

Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it now runs a marketplace where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing a new web browser built specifically for AI agents.

Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs.

Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s newly announced partners haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid expansion , which now includes partnered tools for small businesses , a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway.

“Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”
